things_to_do.title: Recreation Point Day Use
things_to_do.description: Recreation Point is nestled in a partially shaded cove overlooking the northern end of Bass Lake. It offers tent-only, overnight sites and picnic area for groups. The maximum group sizes range from 30-50 people per campsite and 50-100 people per picnic site. The camp consists of four sites on one loop: Knoll, Lagoon, Scout and Acorn. The group picnic areas, Cove, Oak Point and South Park, are on a separate loop.

things_to_do.title: Trails End Picnic Area
things_to_do.description: At the end of the road, Trails End Picnic Site is located past Dinkey Creek Campground. It offers several picnic sites, two vault toilets, and great place to swim and hang out under the sun.

things_to_do.title: Helms Picnic Site
things_to_do.description: Located at Wishon Reservoir, Helms Picnic areas offers 10 sites for day use. Sites accommodate up to 6 people and each have picnic tables.Vault toilets are provided.

things_to_do.description: North side of Merced River. River access. Oaks. Pines. River rafting - steps near to the river. River current unpredictable. Watch out for rattlesnakes and poison oak.

things_to_do.description: Located on the east side of Dinkey Creek. Picnic site is located on large sandy flat above Dinkey Creek. Good shade provide from cedar and pine trees. Provides fisherman access to Dinkey Creek. Stoves: Yes, grill- NO FIRES

things_to_do.description: Located at the west end near the Huntington Lake Dam, Dowville Picnic Area offers several picnic sites shaded by dense fir trees. Vault toilets are provided and each site has a picnic table.

things_to_do.title: Huntington Boat Ramp & Launching Site
things_to_do.description: The Huntington Boat Launching facility offers paved boating access, parking, and day use at Huntington Lake. A small beach and picnic area make this a great place for swimming and relaxing under the sun. Vault toilets are available.

things_to_do.description: Located on Huntington Lake, Bear Cove Picnic Site offers 18 picnic sites shaded by dense fir trees. Drinking water and vault toilets are provided and each site has a picnic table and grill.

The campground is ideal for tents, as well as small RVs. Each campsite has a picnic table, campfire ring and bear-proof food storage locker, all set off a bit from the parking spur. campgrounds.description: Located along the Kaiser Pass Road near the High Sierra Ranger Station. Bosillo Creek runs adjacent to campground. There are 3 available first-come, first-serve campsites. campgrounds.description: Located along Jackass Creek, Bowler Group Campground offers 12 campsites and a primitive amphitheater. The campground provides one vault toilet and each campsite has a table and fire ring. Horses are permitted; however, facilities are not available.

campgrounds.description: Shaded by dense pine trees, Swanson Campground is located near the town of Shaver Lake. Paved and dirt roads provide access to the campground. There is a vault toilet and each site has a table, fire ring and grill. A Campground Host is also on site. Visitors can experience a wide variety of recreational activities such as fishing, boating, and hiking at nearby Shaver Lake.

campgrounds.description: Situated on the north side of the Merced River, Dry Gulch Campground is a small camp that features walk-in tent sites on the river. Chilkoot is named for the creek that runs by the campground. Campground is accessible only by Off Highway Vehicles.

Paved and dirt roads provided access to the campground. Large RV's or motorhomes not recommended for travel on Kaiser Pass Road.

campgrounds.description: Located on a hillside overlooking Bass Lake, Forks Campground has huge Ponderosa Pines that create a majestic setting for a fantastic camping experience. campgrounds.description: Laid out in a single loop along Chiquito Creek, Sweetwater Campground is shaded by pine, oak and cedar trees. things_to_do.title: Lower Cave Tour
things_to_do.description: In 1924, National Geographic expedition members wrote about the wonders of Lower Cave. Visitors today can see the evidence left behind from those and other explorers.
things_to_do.image_caption: Gigantic stalactites are one of the many formations you'll see on the Lower Cave Tour.

things_to_do.title: King's Palace Tour
things_to_do.description: The King's Palace Tour takes visitors through four highly decorated chambers and the deepest portion of the cavern open to the public.
things_to_do.image_caption: Visitors enjoy the Queen's Chamber on the ranger-guided King's Palace Tour.

things_to_do.title: Walnut Canyon Desert Drive
things_to_do.description: Discover canyon views, desert plants, and wildlife along this unpaved road.
things_to_do.image_caption: Walnut Canyon Desert Drive

things_to_do.title: Guadalupe Ridge Trail (GRT)
things_to_do.description: This trail covers 100 miles (161 km) through Carlsbad Caverns National Park, Lincoln National Forest, Bureau of Land Management, and Guadalupe Mountains National Park. Over 20 miles (32 km) of this trail is within Carlsbad Caverns National Park.
things_to_do.image_caption: View of the desert landscape along the Guadalupe Ridge Trail.

things_to_do.title: Rattlesnake Springs Picnic Area
things_to_do.description: Have a relaxing picnic among tall cottonwood trees and watch for a variety of birds.
things_to_do.image_caption: Picnic tables under large cottonwood trees at Rattlesnake Springs.

things_to_do.title: Chihuahuan Desert Nature Trail
things_to_do.description: Enjoy views of the Guadalupe Mountains and explore Chihuahuan Desert plant life along this short 0.7 mile (1.1 km) loop trail.

things_to_do.description: Enjoy the Chihuahuan Desert in a serene landscape along this 3.5 mile (5 km) trail.
things_to_do.image_caption: The Chihuahuan Desert and mountains along the Juniper Ridge Trail.

things_to_do.description: This 3.7 miles (6km) trail descends the escarpment, ending at the White's City campground.
things_to_do.image_caption: Hikes on the Old Guano Trail.

things_to_do.image_caption: Views and desert plants along the Yucca Canyon Trail.

things_to_do.description: Follow down a canyon for 3 miles (4.8 km) and enjoy a variety of Chihuahuan Desert plants.

things_to_do.description: The Big Room and Natural Entrance trails can be enjoyed at your own pace. The Big Room Trail is easy to moderate in difficulty. The Natural Entrance Trail is strenuous. Enjoy one or both to experience a variety of cave formations.

visitor_centers.description: >> RESERVATIONS REQUIRED to enter cavern and must be purchased at recreation.gov or by calling 877-444-6777. The reservation is only for selecting the entry time. Entrance tickets will need to be purchased at the visitor center. << The visitor center offers many services, including a bookstore, gift shop, cafeteria, restrooms, a park movie, information desk, ticket counter, and hands-on educational exhibits.
visitor_centers.image_caption: A variety of interactive exhibits and films are available in the visitor center.
visitor_centers.directions: To access Carlsbad Caverns National Park's only entrance road, New Mexico Highway 7, turn north from U.S. Hwy 62/180 at White's City, New Mexico—which is 20 miles (32 km) southwest of Carlsbad, New Mexico and 145 miles (233 km) northeast of El Paso, Texas. The entrance road stretches a scenic seven miles (11 km) from the park gate at White's City to the visitor center and cavern entrance. The park's visitor center is located 25 miles (40 km) from the town of Carlsbad.

events.title: Bat Flight Program
events.description: Please join us for the free Bat Flight Program (April through October), an evening ranger talk about bats prior to their flight. No reservations are required for this program that occurs every evening from April through October. The program takes place at the Bat Flight Amphitheater, located at the Natural Entrance to Carlsbad Cavern. The start time for the program changes as the summer progresses and sunset times change. Programs may be cancelled in the event of lightning.

events.location: The seating area where you will sit to watch the bats is located at the Natural Entrance to Carlsbad Cavern, about a five minute walk from the visitor center.

things_to_do.title: 8-Mile Loop Trail
things_to_do.description: Covering the majority of the sites on the east side of the park, the 8-Mile Loop Trail provides hikers with a good challenge and rewards them with all of the best scenic points along the mountain ridge.
things_to_do.image_caption: Summer foliage at Chimney Rock.

things_to_do.title: Cabin Camping
things_to_do.description: Lodging in the park can facilitate groups both large and small.
things_to_do.image_caption: Cabin camping in the park offers the opportunity to reserve historic lodges.

things_to_do.title: Fishing at Lewis Pond
things_to_do.description: The Lewis Pond offers a quiet and peaceful opportunity to go freshwater fishing.
things_to_do.image_caption: The Lewis Pond is a peaceful spot to fish.

things_to_do.title: Fly Fishing
things_to_do.description: Big Hunting Creek is a catch-and-return, fly fishing stream.
things_to_do.image_caption: Big Hunting Creek only permits fly fishing.

things_to_do.title: Rock Climbing
things_to_do.description: Wolf Rock is the only location on site open to technical rock climbing.
things_to_do.image_caption: When climbing on Wolf Rock, be fully equipped and prepared.

things_to_do.title: Deerfield Nature Trail
things_to_do.description: This 1.3 mile loop trail travels along Owens Creek, exploring the historical and ecological importance of the area.
things_to_do.image_caption: The Deerfield Nature Trail is a gentle hike around Owens Creek.

things_to_do.title: Brown's Farm Trail
things_to_do.description: The Brown's Farm Trail is a mostly flat, half-mile loop trail that passes through several different forest ecosystems and the remains of an early 1900s farmstead.
things_to_do.image_caption: Portions of the Brown's Farm Trail walk along a boardwalk over streams.

things_to_do.title: Charcoal Exhibit Trail
things_to_do.description: This one-half mile loop trail will take you along several exhibits and displays that will tell the story of the once thriving charcoal making industry on the mountain.
things_to_do.image_caption: Collier huts and charcoal hearths once dotted the mountainside.

things_to_do.title: Spicebush Trail
things_to_do.description: The Spicebush Trail is a short informative walk with wayside panels describing the ever-changing forests at Catoctin Mountain Park.
things_to_do.image_caption: The Spicebush Trail is wheelchair accessible.

things_to_do.title: Blue Blazes Whiskey Still Trail
things_to_do.description: As you travel along the Blue Blazes creek, interpretive trailside signs explore stream ecology and the history of whiskey production on Catoctin Mountain during the time of Prohibition. The trail concludes at an actual whiskey still.
things_to_do.image_caption: The historical whiskey still exhibit lies at the end of the trail.

things_to_do.title: Birdwatching - Brown's Farm Trail
things_to_do.description: Birds can be observed throughout the entire park, but the secluded nature of the west side makes it ideal for birdwatching.
things_to_do.image_caption: Various species of birds can be found throughout the park year-round.

things_to_do.title: Hike to Chimney Rock: The Orange Blazed Trail
things_to_do.description: Chimney Rock reaches a maximum elevation of 1419 ft and Wolf Rock has an elevation of 1401 ft. Great for a romantic hike for that offers opportunities to get back in touch with nature and time to reflect on natures peacefulness and beauty.
things_to_do.image_caption: Fall foliage at Chimney Rock.

things_to_do.title: Hike to the Falls and Hog Rock: The Yellow Blazed Trail
things_to_do.description: This loop is a moderate hike with uphill and downhill sections of the trail that include moderate to steep inclines. This trail is the longest loop (without making any variations) and features Maryland’s largest cascading waterfall at 78 feet and two stunning vistas. The Hog Rock Vista is the highest elevation overlook on any of the trails/loops reaching 1610 ft. Expect hills, uneven surfaces, and rocky terrain along this loop trail.
things_to_do.image_caption: Cunningham Falls is the largest cascading waterfall in Maryland.

things_to_do.title: Hike to Thurmont Vista: The Pink Blazed Trail
things_to_do.description: Thurmont Vista Overlook, the highlight of the Pink Trail, reaches a maximum elevation of 1,499 ft. A moderate hike, traversing the mountainside, this trail provides hikers an opportunity to experience the second growth forests that cover the park.
things_to_do.image_caption: Thurmont Vista is a moderate challenge for hikers seeking a view.

things_to_do.title: Tent Camping
things_to_do.description: Catoctin Mountain has multiple traditional camping options for various group sizes.
things_to_do.image_caption: Owens Creek Campground is a popular tent campsite on the west side of the park.

things_to_do.title: Picnic Areas
things_to_do.description: Catoctin Mountain Park offers many places for individuals to sit down and enjoy a meal under the forest canopy.
things_to_do.image_caption: The Owens Creek Picnic Area is a great spot to relax.

things_to_do.title: Park Museum
things_to_do.description: Step inside the visitor center to walk through the park museum exhibits.
things_to_do.image_caption: The visitor center provides a glimpse into the park's history.

things_to_do.title: Catoctin Junior Ranger Program
things_to_do.description: Come explore Catoctin Mountain Park with our Junior Ranger Book!
things_to_do.image_caption: Become a Jr Ranger At Catoctin Mountain Park!

things_to_do.title: Horse Riding
things_to_do.description: Public riding is not permitted on any trails in the park other than the designated public horse trail.
things_to_do.image_caption: The west side of the park is a popular trail riding destination.

things_to_do.title: Orienteering
things_to_do.description: If you would like to practice your orienteering skills, the park maintains courses that are available for public use.
things_to_do.image_caption: Test your orienteering skills off the beaten path.

things_to_do.title: Cross-Country Skiing
things_to_do.description: Generally, the best skiing is along certain sections of park roads which are closed to vehicular traffic.
things_to_do.image_caption: Even Park Rangers hit the trail to ski.

things_to_do.title: Catoctin Junior Angler Program
things_to_do.image_caption: Explore and see what it takes to be a Jr Angler!

guided.title: Chimney Rock & Wolf Rock Trail Loop
guided.description: This 3.9 mile loop traverses the most difficult sections of trail in the park and allows hikers to experience the impressive views and geological formations at Chimney Rock and Wolf Rock.
guided.image_caption: Chimney Rock provides an excellent view of the ridge and Frederick Valley.

guided.title: Cunningham Falls, Hog Rock, & Blue Ridge Summit Trail Loop
guided.description: This loop is a moderate hike with uphill and downhill sections of the trail that include moderate to steep inclines. This trail is the longest loop (without making any variations) and features Maryland’s largest cascading waterfall at 78 feet and two stunning vistas. The Hog Rock Vista is the highest elevation overlook on any of the trails/loops reaching 1610 ft. Expect hills, uneven surfaces, and rocky terrain along this loop trail. Wolf Rock, Chimney Rock, & Hog Rock formations are pet free areas.
guided.image_caption: Hog Rock stands at 1610 ft, the highest view in the park.

guided.title: Deerfield Nature Trail: A Story of Natural Resources
guided.description: The Deerfield Nature Trail takes you through a rich cultural history from American Indians gathering resources for stone tools to early European settlers homesteading in the area to start a new life. This 1.3 mile loop trail will reflect on the resources that were used to help people survive and thrive.
guided.image_caption: Deerfield Nature Trail is a great hike for families.

guided.title: Ever-Changing Ecosystems: Brown's Farm Trail Loop
guided.description: The Brown's Farm Trail is a mostly flat, half-mile loop trail that passes through several different forest ecosystems and the remains of an early 1900s farmstead.
guided.image_caption: The Brown's Farm Trail provides a peaceful walk through the mountains diverse forest ecosystems.

guided.title: History and Nature: Blue Blazes Whiskey Still Trail
guided.description: The Blue Blazes Whiskey Still Trail is a place where nature and history come together in harmony.
guided.image_caption: A whiskey still exhibit, common to what was once seen in the Appalachians, stands along the stream.

guided.title: Industry on the Mountain: Charcoal Exhibit Trail
guided.description: Located at one of the numerous peaks of Catoctin Mountain, and approximately one mile north of the Visitor Center, the Charcoal Exhibit tells the story of how once the mountain belched smoke and was lit with seemingly ceaseless fires. This half mile hike is easily accessed from the Thurmont Vista Parking Area as well as from nearby hiking trails. Step back in history and learn of the history of the Charcoal Industry on Catoctin Mountain.
guided.image_caption: The Charcoal Trail provides a glimpse into the mountain's history

visitor_centers.title: Visitor Center
visitor_centers.description: The visitor center hosts new exhibits, installed in spring 2019. Learn about the history of Catoctin Mountain and the national park that was created here. American Indians, farmers, iron makers, the WPA, CCC, Jobs Corps and so many others played a role in making Catoctin Mountain Park the special place it is today. Discover how even your visit plays a part in the making of this park. Eastern National provides a small sales area with items to help you remember your visit.
visitor_centers.image_caption: Catoctin Mountain Park's visitor center during the summer with a flourishing pollinator garden.
visitor_centers.directions: To reach the visitor center from the east, follow US Route 15 to MD Route 77 and go west about 3 miles. The visitor center is on the right side of the road. From the west, take I 70 to MD 66 at exit 35. Turn left onto MD 66 north and travel about 5 miles, passing through the roundabout. Turn right onto MD 64 and drive 1 mile. Turn right onto MD 77. Drive on MD 77 about 7.5 miles. The visitor center is on the left.
visitor_centers.operating_hours: Visitor Center: The Visitor Center is currently open from 9am-4:30pm and features a small exhibit, store, restrooms, and trail advice.

campgrounds.title: Adirondack Shelters
campgrounds.description: Reservations Required. No Walk Ins. Available year-round, the Adirondack Shelters located near the northern most point of the park, provide a destination for true nature immersion and an alternative to drive-up camping. There are two shelters that offer the bare minimum with regard to outdoor accommodation. A moderate three-mile uphill hike over rocky and gently rolling terrain starting at Camp Round Meadow will lead you to these three-sided shelters.
campgrounds.image_caption: Two 3-sided shelters offer back-country solitude for hike-in campers.
campgrounds.operating_hours: Adirondack Shelters Rental Information: The Adirondack shelters are available year round.

campgrounds.title: Camp Greentop
campgrounds.description: Located on the National Register of Historic Places, Camp Greentop is a perfect location for organized groups to hold large events, retreats, or conferences. The camp has space for 150 people to sleep on twin beds. There are 12 cabins that sleep 10 each, one lodge that sleeps 12, and three smaller cabins. Recent upgrades include a new swimming pool, renovated Dining and Recreation Halls, and upgraded electrical systems including new outlets and ceiling fans in each of the guest cabins.
campgrounds.image_caption: The Camp Greentop Office features a colorful totem poll.
campgrounds.operating_hours: Camp Greentop: Reservations available in early May and mid-August through October. Please contact the Camp Manager for more information.

campgrounds.title: Camp Misty Mount
campgrounds.description: Advanced reservations required. Camp Misty Mount is a cabin rental facility for individuals, families, or small groups. This historic cabin camp was completed in 1937 by the Works Progress Administration. The camp is surrounded by hardwood forests on the slopes of Catoctin Mountain Park. Recent upgrades to Camp Misty Mount include a renovated swimming pool and bath house, new cots and mattresses, and upgraded electrical systems including new outlets and ceiling fans in each of the guest cabins.
campgrounds.image_caption: Enjoy a stay in one of the rustic cabins at Camp Misty Mount.
campgrounds.operating_hours: Camp Misty Mount: Open for reservations May - October

campgrounds.title: Camp Round Meadow
campgrounds.description: Advanced reservations required. Camp Round Meadow accommodates up to 120 guests in 4 heated dorms that sleep 30 people each. Each dorm has bathrooms with flush toilets, hot showers, and electric outlets. Additional facilities include a dining hall, gymnasium, classrooms, a conference room, outdoor fire pit, and a small outdoor gazebo. Recent upgrades include renovated restrooms in the dorms and a new HVAC system in the gym.
campgrounds.operating_hours: Camp Round Meadow: Open for reservations mid-March through mid-December

campgrounds.title: Owens Creek Campground
campgrounds.description: Advanced reservations required. Owens Creek Campground offers family camping in a wooded setting. There are 50 sites, 3 have ADA features. Maximum trailer length is 22 feet. One vehicle is permitted per site. There are no hook-ups. Use of alcohol is prohibited. Pets allowed and must leashed and tended to at all time. Tent pads have been updated and expanded to a minimum size of 12' x 12'. See reservations page for more details on each site.
campgrounds.image_caption: The campground entrance is on Foxville Deerfield Road.
campgrounds.operating_hours: Owens Creek Campground: Open for servations May through October.

campgrounds.title: Poplar Grove Youth Group Tent Campground
campgrounds.description: Reservations Required. No Walk-Ins. Poplar Grove is open to adult supervised organized youth groups whose members are under age 18. There are 3 sites within Poplar Grove. Each site accommodates up to 25 persons. Groups share pit toilets and a pavilion. Each site has picnic tables, grills and a fire circle.
campgrounds.image_caption: Poplar Grove Tent Area Site A
campgrounds.operating_hours: Poplar Grove Youth Group Tent Campground: Open for reservations April - November

events.title: Commercialized Catoctin: From Industrialization to Recreation
events.description: Join a park intern capstone program on Saturday August 8, at 1:00 P.M. for a guided hiking tour on the fall of Catoctin’s Iron Industry and its rebirth as a National Park from logging and tourism. The program will last 30 minutes and will begin at the Thurmont Vista Parking Area, following the Charcoal Trail for approximately .5 miles. Please bring comfortable walking shoes, water, and appropriate clothing for an outdoor program.
events.image_caption: Commercialized Catoctin: From Industrialization to Recreation
events.location: Program will start at the Thurmont Vista Parking Lot area, approximately 1-mile on Park Central Road from Catoctin Visitor Center. For mapping apps please use this address to reach the visitor center and then follow Park Central Road from there. 14707 Park Central Road Thurmont, MD 21788

events.title: National Junior Ranger Day
events.description: Join us for a day full of Junior Ranger activities and programs at Catoctin Mountain Park! summary.short_description: Channel Islands National Park encompasses five remarkable islands and their ocean environment, preserving and protecting a wealth of natural and cultural resources. Isolation over thousands of years has created unique animals, plants, and archeological resources found nowhere else on Earth and helped preserve a place where visitors can experience coastal southern California as it once was.

guided.title: Anacapa Island: Self-Guided Tour
guided.description: There are two possible routes for this tour. Both routes begin at the visitor center. You may take the lower trail located in front of the buildings, which leads to Cathedral Cove. Or you may take the upper trail located behind the buildings, which leads to Pinniped Point. Both routes cover the same information. For variety, we recommend you take the opposite route back.

guided.title: Mainland Visitor Center: Native Plant Garden Tour—Guide to Island Chumash Plant Usage
guided.description: The Native Plant Garden includes some of the important plants used by the island Chumash. Each trail station includes a brief discussion of these plants and the uses made of them by the Chumash. Stations along the trail are marked by numbered tiles and decorated with a brown Chumash symbol.

guided.title: Mainland Visitor Center: Native Plant Garden Tour—Guide to Island Plant Adaptations
guided.description: A fascinating variety of plants can be found in California’s Channel Islands National Park. The distance and isolation of the islands from the mainland has allowed plants and animals to develop into unique island forms. Trail stops describing these unique plants and adaptations are marked by numbered posts and decorated with a leaf shape.

guided.title: San Miguel Island: Self-Guided Tour
guided.description: This tour provides 5 interpretive stops along the 1.5 mile hike (one-way) to the ranger station. Due to unexploded ordnance, you may only hike on your own to Cuyler Harbor beach, Nidever Canyon, Cabrillo monument, Lester ranch site and the ranger station. Visitors are required to stay on the designated island trail system. No off-trail hiking is permitted. Entering other areas without a ranger is a violation of federal law.

guided.title: Santa Barbara Island: Arch Point Self-Guided Tour
guided.description: This tour provides 7 interpretive stops along the 4 mile loop to Arch Point including a stop at Elephant Seal Cove.

guided.title: Santa Barbara Island: Signal Peak Self-Guided Tour
guided.description: This tour provides 7 interpretive stops along the 3 mile loop to Signal Peak including a stop at the Seal Lion Rookery.

guided.title: Santa Cruz Island: Cavern Point Self-Guided Tour
guided.description: This tour includes six interpretive stops along the one-mile walk from Scorpion Beach to Cavern Point.

guided.title: Santa Cruz Island: Prisoners Harbor Self-Guided Tour
guided.description: The tour provides five interpretive stops along the short one-mile loop walk from Prisoners Beach to the Navy Road Overlook. For information on other areas throughout Prisoners Harbor please click on those individual sites.

guided.title: Santa Cruz Island: Scorpion Ranch Farm Implements Self-Guided Tour
guided.description: Learn about the variety of historic farm implements around Scorpion Ranch.

guided.title: Santa Rosa Island: Cherry Canyon Self-Guided Tour
guided.description: This tour provides eight interpretive stops along the 1.75-mile walk from the pier to Water Canyon Beach via Cherry Canyon. Before you leave the ranch area, make sure to visit the ranch exhibit in the schoolhouse.
guided.image_caption: Cherry Canyon Trail, Santa Rosa Island

things_to_see.title: A Window Into Their World
things_to_see.description: Stop 3: Signal Peak Tour Throughout your hike today, you may discover tiny fragments of broken shells glittering in the soil or piles of shells falling out from the cliff edge. How did these shells get there? It must be the ocean at work-or is it?Archeologists identify these sites as "middens," debris piles containing remnants of past societies-the Tongva, the Chumash, and their ancestors.

things_to_see.title: Abalone Rocks Marsh
things_to_see.description: Just north of East Point is Abalone Rocks Marsh, the second largest wetland on the northern islands (Prisoners Harbor wetland on Santa Cruz is the largest).

things_to_see.title: Airstrip
things_to_see.description: In a flyer's eyes, Santa Rosa Island is blessed with a number of suitable flat areas for landing small planes, but the owners restricted flights and landings throughout their tenure. The Vails and others started flying over to the island in the 1930s, landing on a section of hay field southeast of the ranch house, which eventually developed into the "official" landing strip on the island.

things_to_see.title: Anacapa Island Landing Dock
things_to_see.description: Since Anacapa is a cliff island, access to top is only at the Landing Cove on East Anacapa. Visitors must climb from the boat up a steel-rung ladder to a dock. Once ashore, visitors must climb 157 stairs to the top of the island.

things_to_see.title: Anacapa Island Webcam
things_to_see.description: The Anacapa Island Webcam provides incredible views of the park's iconic symbol Arch Rock, seabird rookeries, and the historic lighthouse, as well as the ocean life and sea conditions at the landing cove and nearby waters.

things_to_see.title: Anacapa Island — 'anyapax
things_to_see.description: 'anyapax is the Chumash word for Anacapa. It means mean 'mirage' or 'illusion' and refers to the atmospheric phenomena that occasionally distorts the appearance of the island when viewed from the mainland. Almost five miles long, these islets (appropriately named East, Middle, and West Anacapa Islands) have a total land area of about one square mile (700 acres). Waves have eroded the volcanic island, creating towering sea cliffs, sea caves, and natural bridges.

things_to_see.title: Arch Point
things_to_see.description: This one-mile, round trip hike from the visitor center offers wildflowers in season and great coastal views of Arch Point. This arch on the northeast shore of the island is a 130 ft tall and was created by wave erosion of fault weakened rock.

things_to_see.title: Arch Point Hike
things_to_see.description: Incredible sunsets, coastal views, and wildflowers in season are the reward for the one-mile, round-trip hike to Arch Point. Distance: 1 mile (round trip from visitor center) Difficulty: Moderate

things_to_see.title: Arch Rock — pasawapʰ hoti or ’aɬwaštimot̓o
things_to_see.description: pasawapʰ hoti is the Chumash word for Arch Rock. It means 'house of the cormorant.' Arch Rock was also known as ’aɬwaštimot̓o. Waves have eroded the volcanic island, creating towering sea cliffs, sea caves, and natural bridges, including forty-foot-high Arch Rock-a symbol of Anacapa and Channel Islands National Park.

things_to_see.title: Backcountry Beach Camping Northwest Quadrant
things_to_see.description: Primitive, dispersed backcountry beach camping is available in the Norththwest Quadrant (Sandy Point to Carrington Point) from September 16 through December 31.

things_to_see.title: Backcountry Beach Camping Southeast Quadrant
things_to_see.description: Primitive, dispersed backcountry beach camping is available in the Southeast Quadrant (East Point to South Point) from August 15 through December 31. Learn more at:

things_to_see.title: Backcountry Beach Camping Southwest Quadrant
things_to_see.description: Primitive, dispersed backcountry beach camping is available in the Southwest Quadrant (South Point to Sandy Point) from September 16 through December 31.

things_to_see.title: Bald Eagle Webcams
things_to_see.description: The Bald Eagle Webcams provide an intimate view of the breeding and nesting behavior of bald eagles at the Channel Islands.

things_to_see.title: Be A Channel Islands Junior Ranger
things_to_see.description: This program helps children discover and protect the wonders of the islands. Ask for a free junior ranger booklet at the visitor center or boat/plane concessionaire offices or on the islands from park staff.

things_to_see.title: Becher's Bay
things_to_see.description: Becher's Bay is the main port of entry to Santa Rosa Island. The bay provides some protection from the strong northwest winds. The bay contains a pier and beautiful, wind-swept, white-sand beach.

things_to_see.title: Becher's Bay Coastal Trail Hike
things_to_see.description: A flat walk along coastal bluffs with great views. Connects with the coastal road near the airstrip with access to Water Canyon Campground, Water Canyon Beach, and other destinations. Be aware of planes as the airstrip is active. Distance: 2 miles (round trip from pier to airstrip junction) Difficulty: Easy

things_to_see.title: Becher's Bay Pier
things_to_see.description: Boat visitors must climb from the boat up a steel-rung ladder to a pier at Becher's Bay on Santa Rosa Island. When the pier is closed, landings are via skiff onto the beach. For nearly 150 years, Santa Rosa Island owners maintained a pier to accommodate shipping cattle, sheep, and supplies. The first pier on Santa Rosa Island was constructed in June 1859, presumably at Bechers Bay near or at the present site of the pier.

things_to_see.title: Biosecurity
things_to_see.image_caption: Protect your park by conducting a biosecurity check before departing the mainland.

things_to_see.title: Bird Watching
things_to_see.description: The Channel Islands support a rich variety of birds, distinct in many ways from the birds of the adjacent mainland. The islands offer protected habitat in an increasingly disturbed southern California environment.

things_to_see.title: Black Mountain
things_to_see.description: The highest peak (1298 feet) on the northeast side of the island provides stunning views to visitors willing to make the strenuous 8-mile rountrip hike.

things_to_see.title: Black Mountain Hike
things_to_see.description: A long, steep climb that rewards visitors with oak woodlands and great views (weather permitting) of Santa Rosa, San Miguel, Santa Cruz, and the mainland. Visitors may make this a loop hike by including the Cherry Canyon trail and Telephone and Soledad roads. Distance: 8 miles (round trip from pier) Difficulty: Strenuous

things_to_see.title: Blacksmith Shop (Scorpion Ranch)
things_to_see.description: Archeological excavations around and within this building revealed artifacts and materials that suggested that this may have been the location of the"forge" or blacksmith shop shown on an 1892 map.

things_to_see.title: Blacksmith Shop Barn and Matanza Boilers
things_to_see.description: This building has been called the blacksmith shop, freezer barn, generator barn, and a barn-utility building. It was probably constructed in the early 1870s and housed the original blacksmith shop and other workshops and utility areas.

things_to_see.title: Buffalo Hay Baler
things_to_see.description: Hay balers were first built in the 1850s. Except for the efforts of a few individuals, hay presses were given little attention for another two decades. Even then the development of hay presses came very slowly. The early balers such as this Buffalo were primarily designed for the needs of small farmers, requiring small capital outlay, besides the advantage of being a one or two-man operation. The original bunkhouse, actually a complex of three buildings-the foreman's residence, the bunkhouse, and the cookhouse-had been built either by Alpheus Thompson in 1855 or by the More family around 1870.It was described by Edward Vail in 1901 as a "large two-story ranch house" and was used by Vail & Vickers to house the foreman and the crew's dining room. things_to_see.title: Cabrillo Monument
things_to_see.description: The Cabrillo Civic Clubs erected a monument in the form of a pile of stones and prehistoric stone artifacts topped by an inscribed granite cross on a knoll near the old shearing sheds in 1937.

things_to_see.title: Cabrillo Monument Hike
things_to_see.description: In 1542, Juan Rodriguez Cabrillo became the first European to explore the Channel Islands. A monument honoring him was erected above Cuyler Harbor in 1937. Distance: 2 miles (round trip from Cuyler Harbor) Difficulty: Strenuous (due to short, steep climb to top of island)

things_to_see.title: Caliche Forest
things_to_see.description: Due to unexploded ordnance, visitors must be accompanied by a ranger to this location. Entering this area without a ranger is a violation of federal law. The San Miguel Island's isolation has helped to preserve one of the island's most interesting features-the caliche forest, calcified casts of ancient vegetation that have been exposed in several areas by the eroding sand. things_to_see.title: Caliche Forest Hike
things_to_see.description: The caliche forest is a naturally occurring geologic feature consisting of prehistoric vegetation that has calcified, forming a "fossilized" landscape. Distance: 5 miles (round trip from Cuyler Harbor) Difficulty: Strenuous

things_to_see.title: Cardwell Point
things_to_see.description: Due to unexploded ordnance, visitors must be accompanied by a ranger to this location. Entering this area without a ranger is a violation of federal law. Seals and sea lions can be seen from several viewpoints on San Miguel Island that can be reached on ranger-guided hikes. Northern elephant seals can even be seen on the beach at Cuyler Harbor where visitors land on the island. however, the most famous and diverse pinniped viewing location on San Miguel Island is Point Bennet

things_to_see.title: Cardwell Point Hike
things_to_see.description: The hike to Cardwell Point includes spectacular views of Santa Rosa Island and a seal and sea lion rookery. Distance: 6 miles (round trip from Cuyler Harbor) Difficulty: Strenuous

visitor_centers.title: Channel Islands National Park Visitor Center
visitor_centers.description: The Robert J. Lagomarsino Visitor Center at Channel Islands National Park features a bookstore, a display of marine aquatic life, and exhibits featuring the unique character of each park island. Visitors also will enjoy the 25-minute park movie, “A Treasure in the Sea,” shown throughout the day in the auditorium (closed-caption film available upon request). The fully accessible visitor center is open 8:30 am until 5 pm daily. The visitor center is closed on Thanksgiving and December 25th.
visitor_centers.image_caption: Robert J. Lagomarsino Visitor Center at Channel Islands National Park
visitor_centers.directions: The visitor center is located in the Ventura Harbor in Ventura, California. Ventura is located 70 miles north of Los Angeles and 30 miles south of Santa Barbara. Plane, train, and bus service are all available to Los Angeles and Santa Barbara. Only train, bus, and private car transportation are available from Los Angeles and Santa Barbara to Ventura.
visitor_centers.operating_hours: Channel Islands National Park Visitor Center: The visitor center is open 8:30 am until 5 pm daily. The visitor center is closed on Thanksgiving and December 25th.

Open 10:30 am until 4:30 pm daily. The visitor center is closed on Thanksgiving Day, December 25, January 1, and the first Friday in August for Fiesta.

campgrounds.title: Anacapa Island Campground
campgrounds.description: Primitive camping is available (seven sites; $15 per night per site; reservations required). Picnic table, food storage box, and pit toilet are provided. No water is available. Distance from landing to campground is one-half mile and includes a 157-stair climb. WARNING: Western gulls nest on Anacapa Island From April through mid-August. During this time, visitors will encounter seabird rookery conditions: guano, strong odor, constant noise, bird carcasses, and birds protecting their territory.

campgrounds.title: Santa Cruz Island Del Norte Backcountry Campground
campgrounds.description: The Santa Cruz Island Del Norte Backcountry Campground is currently the only backcountry campground on Santa Cruz Island. The hike to the campground is 3.5 miles from Prisoners Harbor and 12 miles from Scorpion Anchorage. It has four primitive campsites (four persons per site) and users must camp within these designated sites.Reservations are required ($15 per night-per site). A picnic table, food storage box, and pit-style toilet are provided (campers must bring their own toilet paper).

campgrounds.title: Santa Rosa Island Backcountry Beach Camping
campgrounds.description: Backcountry camping on Santa Rosa Island is currently limited to certain beaches between August 15th and December 31st. Hiking is along the beach and rugged, unsigned (and sometimes unmaintained) dirt roads. The closest beach for camping is 8 miles from the boat/plane drop-off location. Reservations are required ($10 per night-per site). No services are provided.This is primitive, dispersed, backcountry camping. Visitors must backpack to all locations and carry all of their own gear, food and water.

events.title: Guided Hikes on the Islands
events.description: On days that the concessionaire boats run to the islands, guided hikes may be offered by national park rangers, volunteers, or concessionaire naturalists. If they are not available to lead hikes, self-guided interpretive trail booklets are available. Guided hike locations, distances, and departure times will be announced after your arrival on the island during the visitor orientation. Please check with a ranger, volunteer, or concessionaire employee for more information.

source_pack.extract: Channel Islands National Park encompasses five remarkable islands and their ocean environment, preserving and protecting a wealth of natural and cultural resources. Isolation over thousands of years has created unique animals, plants, and archeological resources found nowhere else on Earth and helped preserve a place where visitors can experience coastal southern California as it once was.
